question: Move the AED at P.S. 075 Emily Dickinson into a 24/7 outdoor cabinet on the building's street wall.

evidence.text: P.S. 075 Emily Dickinson (School, ZIP 10025) has a registered AED at "Outside Room 307; Main Entrance".
Its hours come from: School building assumed open 7 AM to 6 PM on school days, September to June. Move the school-hours control to test other closing times.
Under that assumption it is reachable 55 of 168 hours in a school-year week, and 0 hours in a summer week if it is a school.
In 2025, an expected 1.2 cardiac-arrest 911 calls a year came from inside its two-minute walking area at hours when every AED in reach was shut (rank 6 of 100 NYC schools).
Within 400 m there are 9 other registered AED locations; 0 of them are open 24/7 by their published hours.
Citywide, a time-blind map puts 4.6% of call-weighted area within a two-minute walk of an AED; at the hour calls actually came in, 1.4% was within reach of one confirmed open.
Published research: a bystander shock with a public AED was associated with survival to discharge of 66.5% versus 43.0% without (Pollack et al., Circulation 2018, observed shockable public arrests).
Overture Maps lists no fire station, police station or hospital within 400 m.
Unknown to this data: cabinet cost, vandalism risk, whether the school already allows after-hours access, and the actual location of each 2025 call inside the ZIP (only ZIP-level data is public).

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: Moving the AED to a 24/7 outdoor cabinet addresses a genuine gap in coverage. The school's current indoor placement is reachable only 55 of 168 hours weekly during the school year, and zero hours in summer [E3]. Last year, the area experienced 1.2 cardiac-arrest calls annually during times when every nearby AED was closed [E4]. Research shows bystander shock with a public AED correlates with 66.5% survival to discharge versus 43.0% without [E7]. With no fire station, police station, or hospital within 400 meters [E8], and no other 24/7 AEDs nearby [E5], this location could meaningfully improve response capability for a high-need area.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate's case rests on incomplete data and unproven assumptions. Yes, the current AED is inaccessible 113 hours weekly during school year [E3], but we don't know the actual location of last year's 1.2 calls—only that they fell in the ZIP code [E9]. They may have been blocks away. The survival research [E7] is compelling, but it compares any bystander shock to none; it doesn't prove an outdoor cabinet here closes a critical gap when nine other AEDs exist within 400 meters [E5]. We lack cabinet costs, vandalism risk, and whether after-hours school access is already possible [E9]. Before installing permanent infrastructure, we need precise call mapping and a cost comparison to simpler alternatives like negotiating school after-hours access.

turns.speaker: advocate
turns.text: The skeptic is right that we lack the precise call locations within the ZIP [E9], and that matters for confirming this specific site is optimal. But the gap itself is real and quantifiable: 1.2 cardiac-arrest calls annually occurred when every reachable AED was closed [E4]. The nine nearby AEDs [E5] don't solve that problem—they were all shut too. The survival research [E7] doesn't require this cabinet to be the only option; it shows that access during those 1.2 events could shift outcomes from 43 percent to 66.5 percent survival. Before cost analysis or negotiating school access, we should map this year's calls to confirm whether the gap persists at this location. That data would justify the cabinet investment.

turns.speaker: skeptic
turns.text: The advocate makes a fair point: the gap is real and measurable—1.2 calls occurred when all nearby AEDs were closed [E4]. But that doesn't yet justify this specific cabinet. We don't know if those calls happened near P.S. 075 or elsewhere in the ZIP [E9]. More critically, we have no cost estimate for the cabinet, no data on vandalism risk, and no confirmation that after-hours school access isn't already negotiable [E9]. Call mapping would help, but so would simply asking whether the school can unlock Room 307 after hours—a far cheaper test of whether the real problem is the AED's location or its access hours.

verdict.summary: Real coverage gap exists (1.2 annual calls during all-closed hours), but precise call location within ZIP unknown. Map 2025 calls and test school after-hours access before cabinet installation.
verdict.strongestFor: 1.2 cardiac arrests yearly occur when all nearby AEDs closed [E4]. Bystander shock correlates with 66.5% vs 43.0% survival [E7].
verdict.strongestAgainst: Actual call locations unknown—may be blocks away [E9]. Nine other AEDs within 400m exist [E5]. Cabinet cost, vandalism risk, and school access alternatives unstudied [E9].
verdict.nextStep: Map 2025 cardiac-arrest calls to confirm proximity to P.S. 075; simultaneously request school's feasibility for after-hours Room 307 access.
